solution:
The colligative property here is the RELATIVE LOWERING OF VAPOUR PRESSURE. For a non-volatile solute, Raoult's law gives \(p = p^\circ x_1\), so the relative lowering equals the mole fraction of the solute:
\(\frac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_2\).
Molar mass of urea \(\text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2 = 2(14) + 4(1) + 12 + 16 = 60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); molar mass of water \(= 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles of solute \(n_2 = \frac{50}{60} = 0.8333\,\text{mol}\); moles of solvent \(n_1 = \frac{850}{18} = 47.22\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_2 = \frac{0.8333}{0.8333 + 47.22} = \frac{0.8333}{48.06} = 0.01734\).
Lowering of vapour pressure: \(p^\circ - p = x_2\,p^\circ = 0.01734 \times 23.8 = 0.413\,\text{mm Hg}\).
\(p = 23.8 - 0.413 = 23.39\,\text{mm Hg}\).
Vapour pressure of water over the solution \(= 23.4\,\text{mm Hg}\); relative lowering of vapour pressure \(= 0.0173\).

The colligative property here is the ELEVATION OF BOILING POINT, \(\Delta T_b = K_b\,m\), where \(K_b\) is the molal elevation constant OF THE SOLVENT. The solvent is water, for which \(K_b = 0.52\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).
At \(750\,\text{mm Hg}\) pure water boils at \(99.63\,^\circ\text{C}\), so at that same pressure the solution must boil \(0.37\,^\circ\text{C}\) higher:
\(\Delta T_b = 100 - 99.63 = 0.37\,\text{K}\).
Molality required: \(m = \frac{\Delta T_b}{K_b} = \frac{0.37}{0.52} = 0.7115\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\).
Mass of solvent \(= 500\,\text{g} = 0.500\,\text{kg}\), so moles of sucrose \(= 0.7115 \times 0.500 = 0.3558\,\text{mol}\).
Molar mass of sucrose \(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} = 12(12) + 22(1) + 11(16) = 342\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= 0.3558 \times 342 = 121.7\,\text{g}\).
Sucrose to be added \(= 121.7\,\text{g}\).

The colligative property here is the DEPRESSION OF FREEZING POINT, \(\Delta T_f = K_f\,m\), where \(K_f\) is the molal depression constant OF THE SOLVENT. The solvent is acetic acid, and the value given for it is \(K_f = 3.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) (not the value for water).
Given \(\Delta T_f = 1.5\,^\circ\text{C} = 1.5\,\text{K}\):
\(m = \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f} = \frac{1.5}{3.9} = 0.3846\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\).
Mass of solvent \(= 75\,\text{g} = 0.075\,\text{kg}\), so moles of ascorbic acid \(= 0.3846 \times 0.075 = 0.02885\,\text{mol}\).
Molar mass of ascorbic acid \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6 = 6(12) + 8(1) + 6(16) = 176\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= 0.02885 \times 176 = 5.08\,\text{g}\).
Mass of ascorbic acid required \(= 5.08\,\text{g}\).

The colligative property here is OSMOTIC PRESSURE, given by the van't Hoff equation \(\pi = \frac{n_2}{V}RT\). A polymer is a non-electrolyte, so no van't Hoff factor is needed.
Moles of polymer: \(n_2 = \frac{1.0}{185000} = 5.405 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{mol}\).
Since the answer is wanted in pascals, work in SI: \(V = 450\,\text{mL} = 0.450\,\text{L} = 4.50 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^3\), \(T = 37 + 273 = 310\,\text{K}\), \(R = 8.314\,\text{Pa m}^3\text{ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\pi = \frac{(5.405 \times 10^{-6})(8.314)(310)}{4.50 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{1.393 \times 10^{-2}}{4.50 \times 10^{-4}}\).
\(\pi = 31.0\,\text{Pa}\).
Osmotic pressure \(= 30.96\,\text{Pa} \approx 31\,\text{Pa}\).

The "pressure" exerted is the vapour pressure of the solution, and the property used is the RELATIVE LOWERING OF VAPOUR PRESSURE. By Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute, \(\frac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_2\).
At the normal boiling point of the solvent the pure solvent's vapour pressure equals \(1\,\text{atm} = 1.013\,\text{bar}\), and \(p = 1.004\,\text{bar}\).
\(x_2 = \frac{1.013 - 1.004}{1.013} = \frac{0.009}{1.013} = 8.885 \times 10^{-3}\).
A \(2\%\) solution by mass contains \(2\,\text{g}\) solute in \(100\,\text{g}\) solution, i.e. in \(98\,\text{g}\) of water.
\(n_1 = \frac{98}{18} = 5.444\,\text{mol}\). Let the molar mass of the solute be \(M_2\), so \(n_2 = \frac{2}{M_2}\).
From \(x_2 = \frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\): \(n_2 = \frac{x_2 n_1}{1 - x_2} = \frac{(8.885 \times 10^{-3})(5.444)}{0.99111} = 0.04880\,\text{mol}\).
\(M_2 = \frac{2}{0.04880} = 41.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar mass of the solute \(= 41\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
_note: Kept the exact mole-fraction relation rather than the dilute approximation x2 = n2/n1. The approximation gives n2 = 0.04837 mol and M2 = 41.35 g/mol, about 1% higher. Both round to ~41 g/mol; flagging in case the printed key quotes 41.35.

solution:
The solute is non-volatile, so Raoult's law gives the vapour pressure of the solution as \(p = p^\circ x_1\), where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of water. Let \(M\) be the molar mass of the solute and \(p^\circ\) the vapour pressure of pure water at \(298\,\text{K}\); write \(a = n_2 = \frac{30}{M}\).
Before adding water: \(n_1 = \frac{90}{18} = 5\,\text{mol}\), so \(2.8 = p^\circ \frac{5}{5 + a}\).
After adding \(18\,\text{g}\) of water: \(n_1 = \frac{108}{18} = 6\,\text{mol}\), so \(2.9 = p^\circ \frac{6}{6 + a}\).
Dividing to eliminate \(p^\circ\): \(\frac{2.8}{2.9} = \frac{5(6 + a)}{6(5 + a)}\), i.e. \(16.8(5 + a) = 14.5(6 + a)\).
\(84 + 16.8a = 87 + 14.5a \Rightarrow 2.3a = 3 \Rightarrow a = 1.304\,\text{mol}\).
(i) \(M = \frac{30}{1.304} = 23.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
(ii) \(p^\circ = 2.8 \times \frac{5 + 1.304}{5} = 2.8 \times 1.2609 = 3.53\,\text{kPa}\).
(i) Molar mass of the solute \(= 23\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); (ii) vapour pressure of pure water at \(298\,\text{K} = 3.53\,\text{kPa}\).

[Textbook note — the data in this question are not physically consistent, though the answer is unaffected. A \(5\%\) (by mass) cane-sugar solution is \(5/342.3\) mol in \(0.095\,\text{kg}\) of water, i.e. \(0.1538\,\text{m}\); a freezing point of \(271\,\text{K}\) is a depression of \(2.15\,\text{K}\) and so implies \(K_f = 13.98\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) for water, against its real value of \(1.86\). With the true \(K_f\) that solution would freeze at \(272.86\,\text{K}\), not \(271\,\text{K}\). The question is posed and answered as a RATIO of the two depressions, in which \(K_f\) cancels, so the printed answer of \(269.07\,\text{K}\) stands and matches the derivation below — but a student checking the given freezing point against a table of \(K_f\) values will find it does not reconcile, and that is the book's inconsistency rather than an error in the answer.] The colligative property is the DEPRESSION OF FREEZING POINT, \(\Delta T_f = K_f\,m\). The solvent is water in both solutions, so \(K_f\) is the same and \(\Delta T_f\) is proportional to the molality.
Both solutions are \(5\%\) by mass, i.e. \(5\,\text{g}\) of solute in \(95\,\text{g}\) of water, so for the same mass of solute the molality is inversely proportional to the molar mass:
\(\frac{\Delta T_f(\text{glucose})}{\Delta T_f(\text{sugar})} = \frac{M(\text{sugar})}{M(\text{glucose})}\).
Molar masses: cane sugar \(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} = 342\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
For cane sugar: \(\Delta T_f = 273.15 - 271 = 2.15\,\text{K}\).
For glucose: \(\Delta T_f = 2.15 \times \frac{342}{180} = 2.15 \times 1.9 = 4.085\,\text{K}\).
Freezing point \(= 273.15 - 4.085 = 269.065\,\text{K}\).
Freezing point of the \(5\%\) glucose solution \(= 269.065\,\text{K} \approx 269.07\,\text{K}\) (i.e. \(-4.085\,^\circ\text{C}\)).
_note: The data are internally inconsistent with real water: molality of the cane-sugar solution is (5/342)/0.095 = 0.1539 mol/kg, so the implied Kf = 2.15/0.1539 = 13.97 K kg/mol, against water's actual 1.86 K kg/mol. The question is nonetheless self-consistent as a ratio problem, which is how it is solved above; the answer does not depend on the absolute Kf.

solution:
The colligative property is the DEPRESSION OF FREEZING POINT. For a mass \(w_2\) of solute in a mass \(w_1\) of solvent, \(\Delta T_f = K_f\,m = \frac{K_f\,w_2 \times 1000}{M_2\,w_1}\), so \(M_2 = \frac{K_f\,w_2 \times 1000}{\Delta T_f\,w_1}\). Here the solvent is benzene, \(K_f = 5.1\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\), \(w_1 = 20\,\text{g}\), \(w_2 = 1\,\text{g}\).
For \(\text{AB}_2\): \(M = \frac{5.1 \times 1 \times 1000}{2.3 \times 20} = \frac{5100}{46} = 110.87\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
For \(\text{AB}_4\): \(M = \frac{5.1 \times 1 \times 1000}{1.3 \times 20} = \frac{5100}{26} = 196.15\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Let the atomic masses be \(\text{A} = a\) and \(\text{B} = b\). Then
\(a + 2b = 110.87\) and \(a + 4b = 196.15\).
Subtracting: \(2b = 85.28\), so \(b = 42.64\).
Hence \(a = 110.87 - 2(42.64) = 25.59\).
Atomic mass of \(\text{A} = 25.59\,\text{u}\); atomic mass of \(\text{B} = 42.64\,\text{u}\).

The colligative property is OSMOTIC PRESSURE, \(\pi = CRT\). Glucose is a non-electrolyte, so no van't Hoff factor is needed, and at a fixed temperature \(\pi\) is directly proportional to the molar concentration.
For the first solution, molar mass of glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(C_1 = \frac{36}{180 \times 1} = 0.20\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) with \(\pi_1 = 4.98\,\text{bar}\).
Hence \(RT = \frac{\pi_1}{C_1} = \frac{4.98}{0.20} = 24.9\,\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\) (consistent with \(R = 0.083\,\text{L bar K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) at \(300\,\text{K}\)).
For the second solution at the same temperature:
\(C_2 = C_1 \times \frac{\pi_2}{\pi_1} = 0.20 \times \frac{1.52}{4.98} = 0.0610\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).
In mass terms this is \(0.0610 \times 180 = 11.0\,\text{g L}^{-1}\).
Concentration \(= 0.061\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\), i.e. about \(11\,\text{g}\) of glucose per litre.

All three are weak monobasic carboxylic acids, so each partly dissociates in water: \(\text{RCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOO}^- + \text{H}^+\). Dissociation raises the number of particles, so the van't Hoff factor is \(i = 1 + \alpha > 1\) and the observed depression is \(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m\). Taken at the same molal concentration in the same solvent, \(K_f\) and \(m\) are fixed, so \(\Delta T_f\) is decided entirely by \(\alpha\), i.e. by the strength of the acid.
The strength is set by the inductive effect of the group attached to \(-\text{COOH}\). In acetic acid the \(\text{CH}_3\) group is electron-releasing \((+I)\), which intensifies the negative charge on the carboxylate ion and destabilises it, so \(\alpha\) is smallest. In trichloroacetic acid the three chlorine atoms are electron-withdrawing \((-I)\); they pull electron density away from the \(\text{O-H}\) bond and disperse the charge of \(\text{CCl}_3\text{COO}^-\), so it ionises far more. Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, so the \(-I\) effect of \(\text{CF}_3\) is stronger still and \(\text{CF}_3\text{COOH}\) is the strongest of the three.
Hence \(\alpha\), and therefore \(i\), increases in the order \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} < \text{CCl}_3\text{COOH} < \text{CF}_3\text{COOH}\), and the observed depression in freezing point increases in exactly that order.
_note: Read "the same amount" as the same molal amount (same number of moles per kg of water), which is what makes the comparison depend only on i. If it meant the same MASS, the molar masses (60, 163.4 and 114 g/mol) would make the molalities differ as well and the trend would not follow from the inductive argument alone.

solution:
The acid \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCOOH}\) is a weak acid, so it dissociates and the observed depression uses the van't Hoff factor: \(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m\), with \(K_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) for the solvent water.
Molar mass \(= \text{C}_4\text{H}_7\text{ClO}_2 = 4(12) + 7(1) + 35.5 + 2(16) = 122.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \frac{10}{122.5} = 0.08163\,\text{mol}\); mass of water \(= 250\,\text{g} = 0.250\,\text{kg}\).
\(m = \frac{0.08163}{0.250} = 0.3265\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\).
For \(\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-\), \(K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}\). Since \(\alpha\) is small, \(\alpha \approx \sqrt{K_a/C}\) with \(C \approx m\) for this dilute aqueous solution:
\(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{1.4 \times 10^{-3}}{0.3265}} = \sqrt{4.288 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.0655\).
One molecule gives two ions, so \(i = 1 + \alpha = 1.0655\) (the extra particles are why the observed depression exceeds the value for an undissociated solute).
\(\Delta T_f = 1.0655 \times 1.86 \times 0.3265 = 0.647\,\text{K}\).
Depression in freezing point \(= 0.65\,\text{K}\) (about \(0.647\,\text{K}\)).
_note: Solving the quadratic exactly instead of using the small-alpha approximation gives alpha = 0.0634, i = 1.0634 and dTf = 0.646 K, i.e. the same answer to two significant figures.

solution:
Fluoroacetic acid is a weak acid, so it dissociates and gives an abnormal (higher than calculated) depression of freezing point: \(\Delta T_f(\text{observed}) = i\,\Delta T_f(\text{calculated})\), with \(\Delta T_f(\text{calculated}) = K_f\,m\) and \(K_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) for the solvent water.
Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_2\text{FCOOH} = \text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{FO}_2 = 2(12) + 3(1) + 19 + 2(16) = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \frac{19.5}{78} = 0.25\,\text{mol}\) in \(0.500\,\text{kg}\) of water, so \(m = 0.50\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\).
\(\Delta T_f(\text{calculated}) = 1.86 \times 0.50 = 0.93\,\text{K}\).
\(i = \frac{\Delta T_f(\text{observed})}{\Delta T_f(\text{calculated})} = \frac{1.0}{0.93} = 1.0753\).
Because each molecule that ionises gives two particles, \(i = 1 + \alpha\), so \(\alpha = 0.0753\). (The observed molar mass would correspondingly be \(78/1.0753 = 72.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), i.e. LOWER than the normal value, which is what dissociation always does.)
For \(\text{CH}_2\text{FCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_2\text{FCOO}^- + \text{H}^+\), taking \(C \approx m = 0.50\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\):
\(K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{0.50 \times (0.0753)^2}{1 - 0.0753} = \frac{2.833 \times 10^{-3}}{0.9247}\).
\(K_a = 3.06 \times 10^{-3}\).
van't Hoff factor \(i = 1.0753\); dissociation constant \(K_a = 3.06 \times 10^{-3}\).

The colligative property is OSMOTIC PRESSURE. \(\text{CaCl}_2\) is an electrolyte, so the van't Hoff factor appears: \(\pi = i\,CRT = i\,\frac{w_2}{M_2 V}RT\). Here \(i = 2.47\) is given (less than the ideal \(3\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^-\), because of ion pairing).
Work in atmospheres, so \(R = 0.0821\,\text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\); \(T = 27 + 273 = 300\,\text{K}\), \(V = 2.5\,\text{L}\), \(\pi = 0.75\,\text{atm}\).
\(C = \frac{\pi}{iRT} = \frac{0.75}{2.47 \times 0.0821 \times 300} = \frac{0.75}{60.84} = 0.01233\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).
Moles required \(= 0.01233 \times 2.5 = 0.03082\,\text{mol}\).
Molar mass of \(\text{CaCl}_2 = 40 + 2(35.5) = 111\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= 0.03082 \times 111 = 3.42\,\text{g}\).
Mass of \(\text{CaCl}_2\) to be dissolved \(= 3.42\,\text{g}\).

The colligative property is OSMOTIC PRESSURE, \(\pi = i\,CRT\). Complete dissociation \(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{K}^+ + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\) gives three ions per formula unit, so \(i = 3\) (this is why the observed molar mass of \(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4\) comes out about one third of its normal value).
Molar mass of \(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 = 2(39) + 32 + 4(16) = 174\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= 25\,\text{mg} = 0.025\,\text{g}\), so moles \(= \frac{0.025}{174} = 1.437 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\).
\(C = \frac{1.437 \times 10^{-4}}{2} = 7.184 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\), \(T = 25 + 273 = 298\,\text{K}\), \(R = 0.083\,\text{L bar K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\pi = 3 \times (7.184 \times 10^{-5}) \times 0.083 \times 298\).
\(\pi = 5.33 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\).
Osmotic pressure \(= 5.33 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\) (equivalently \(5.27 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}\), using \(R = 0.0821\,\text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)).
